title: Effects of gaze control strategies on the impression of robot's internal states

fields.value: Two video-based evaluation experiments and an analysis of human three-party conversation data; the paper also describes a gaze-generation system.

quotes.text: We used a three-party conversation dataset [2], which has also been used in gaze analysis of previous studies [11,38].
We generated 11 patterns of combined head and eye movements (e.g. head 0:eye 10, head 1:eye 9,..., head 10:eye 0; Figure 6) and presented each pattern as a video stimulus (Figure 7).

Two-way mixed ANOVA was conducted to analyze the effects of gaze control types (within-subjects) and robot types (between-subjects) on the impressions of the robot’s thinking behavior and the robot’s extroversion.

fields.value: Online, video-based crowdsourced evaluations; the human conversation dataset consisted of recorded free-topic conversations. A physical laboratory or field setting for the evaluations is not stated.

quotes.text: The dataset consists of multiple sessions of free-topic conversations lasting approximately 25 to 40 min.
Participants took part in the video-based stimulus experiment via crowdsourcing, using their own devices.
We recruited 100 participants thorough a crowd service, and divided them into two groups of 50 participants each.

fields.value: 100 participants in User Study 1 and 100 different participants in User Study 2; 200 participants total across both studies. The analyzed conversation dataset’s total participant count is not stated.

We recruited 100 participants thorough a crowd service, and divided them into two groups of 50 participants each. The participants in this experiment are different from those in the User Study 1.

fields.value: User Study 1: Group A had 32 men and 18 women, mean age 41.2 (SD 7.3); Group B had 35 men and 15 women, mean age 41.4 (SD 9.8). User Study 2: both groups had 26 men and 24 women; mean age 41.5 (SD 8.1) for Group A and 43.5 (SD 10.7) for Group B. Prior robot experience is not stated.

Group A (26 males, 24 females; 41.5 8.1 years old): Viewed only CommU’s videos Group B (26 males, 24 females; 43.5 10.7 years old): Viewed only Nikola’s videos

fields.value: Participants watched video stimuli depicting robots in a triadic dialogue and rated perceived extroversion; in the second study, they rated perceived thinking and extroversion for dialogue videos with thinking intervals. The robot shifted gaze between two people positioned ±30 degrees to its left and right. Study 1 videos lasted about 40 seconds; Study 2 videos lasted about 40–50 seconds.

quotes.text: In this study, we assume a scenario in which a robot shifts its gaze between two people positioned at ±30 degrees to its left and right, respectively.
Each video lasted approximately forty seconds.
Two dialogue scenarios were prepared including intervals where the robot is thinking during its utterances.
The videos lasted approximately forty to fifty seconds.

fields.value: Three participants per depicted interaction: one robot and two human dialogue partners. The paper describes this as a triadic dialogue; the human dataset involved three human participants.

quotes.text: We created videos in which each robot appeared to be one of the three participants in a triadic dialogue.
Each robot was depicted participating in a triadic dialogue, acting as either speaker or listener.
The three participants were seated at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, about two meters side.

fields.value: One robot per depicted interaction; the paper evaluated two robot platforms across separate participant groups.

fields.value: Custom seven-point Likert questionnaire ratings of extroversion in Study 1 and thinking and extroversion in Study 2; video/audio-visual annotation of thinking intervals and gaze behavior in the conversation dataset; NEO-FFI for personality assessment. Statistical analyses included mixed ANOVA and Mann–Whitney U tests.

quotes.text: For each video, participants provided ratings using a seven-point Likert scale on the following item: Personality (Extroversion): ‘Did the robot appear introverted or extroverted?’ (1 very introverted, 4 difficult to decide, 7 very extroverted)

Using a 7-point Likert scale, participants rated each video on: Thinking: ‘Did you feel that the robot behaved as it was thinking during its utterances?’ (1 strongly disagree, 4 difficult to decide, 7 strongly agree) Extroversion: ‘Did the robot appear introverted or extroverted?’ (1 very introverted, 4 difficult to decide, 7 very extroverted)
Furthermore, the NEO-FFI questionnaire [39,40] was used to assess personality traits from a third-person perspective, focusing on the Big Five dimensions.
This annotation process was initially performed by one annotator and subsequently verified by another, both of whom have expertise in dialogue data annotation.

fields.value: Higher head-to-eye ratio (more head movement) increased extroversion ratings; gaze-control type significantly affected perceived thinking and extroversion, with the thinking-aware model scoring higher. Human conversation analysis found significantly different gaze-aversion duration distributions across interval conditions. Statistics are reported in the quotes.

quotes.text: As the proportion of head movement increased, subjective ratings of extroversion tended to increase.
Significant main effects were observed for gaze control type in both thinking (F(1, 98) 51.92, p .01, f 0.72) and extroversion (F(1, 98) 18.85, p .01, f 0.43).

The results confirmed that gaze aversion during cognitive processing effectively conveyed the impression of thinking, and that appropriate gaze aversion could enhance perceptions of extroversion as well.
The comparison between Excluding thinking intervals and During thinking intervals (Recall) showed a significant difference as well (U 719, 196.5, p .001, p 1.91 10−30).

fields.value: The paper frames robotic gaze as a means of expressing internal cognitive states and personality, with gaze behavior in multiparty dialogue organized around participants’ dialogue roles and gaze aversion during thinking.

quotes.text: This study aims to investigate how robots can express internal states through gaze control during multiparty conversations, with a particular focus on the impressions of extroversion and thinking behaviors.
Our ultimate goal is to allow a robot to nonverbally communicate its engagement in cognitive processing through its gaze behavior.
The system targets the control of gaze behavior in three-party conversations.

fields.value: Gaze is controlled according to dialogue roles to direct attention among speaker, addressee, and side participant; gaze aversion during thinking signals cognitive processing, and gaze behavior also contributes to impressions of extroversion.

quotes.text: At the core of the system is the Main Layer, which dynamically determines the appropriate gaze target based on the dialogue roles.
When the system estimates that a participant is engaged in thinking, gaze behavior transitions to reflect this cognitive state such as by breaking eye contact or suspending gaze.
Collectively, these studies underscore the importance of considering dialogue roles in the gaze control mechanisms of dialogue robots.

fields.value: More head movement increased perceived extroversion; with low HER, the humanlike Nikola was rated more introverted than CommU. Thinking-aware gaze control increased perceived thinking and slightly increased extroversion. In the human data, gaze aversion was more frequent and longer during thinking, with upward aversion particularly associated with recall.

quotes.text: As the proportion of head movement increased, subjective ratings of extroversion tended to increase.
Analysis of human conversational data demonstrated that, during cognitive processing, both the duration and frequency of gaze aversion increases.

The results confirmed that gaze aversion during cognitive processing effectively conveyed the impression of thinking, and that appropriate gaze aversion could enhance perceptions of extroversion as well.

Additionally, under conditions of low HER, CommU elicited a significantly higher impression of extroversion compared to Nikola, a finding likely attributable to CommU’s relatively larger eyes and reduced dominance of gaze control.

fields.value: A dialogue-role based gaze model selects gaze targets; a personality adjustment layer and thinking layer modify behavior; a synthesis layer determines target, duration, aversion, direction, and head-to-eye ratio. Gaze motions were model controlled in video stimuli, with speech-driven lip and pitch motion. No sensing or Wizard-of-Oz operation is described.

quotes.text: To accommodate such individual differences, the system adjusts the output of the Main Layer based on each participant’s Personality, enabling the generation of more personalized gaze behaviors.
The final gaze behavior is determined by the Synthesis Layer, which integrates outputs from both the Main Layer and the Thinking Layer.

The robot motions were controlled so that lip motion and head pitch motion is automatically controlled based on speech-driven methods [1,2], and the head yaw and eyeball pitch and yaw movements related to gazing are controlled by the dialogue-role based gaze control model [11].
This model uses different distribution parameters for the dialogue-role-based model in thinking and non-thinking intervals, determined from the multi-party dialogue data analyzes.

fields.value: The study used CommU, a stylized, deformed social conversational robot, and Nikola, a highly humanlike android. CommU has large exaggerated eyes with strong black-white contrast; Nikola has smaller, more realistic eyes.

quotes.text: two robots with distinct appearances a highly human-like android robot Nikola and a stylized, deformed-type robot CommU
We employed both a stylized social conversational robot (CommU) and a humanlike android robot (Nikola), as in User Study 1.
CommU, as a stylized robot with large, exag- gerated eyes and strong black white contrast
Nikola, being a highly human-like android with smaller, more realistic eyes

fields.value: At low HER, Nikola was perceived as more introverted than CommU; authors suggest CommU’s larger, high-contrast eyes may make it seem to be looking at observers across a wider range of gaze directions, reducing sensitivity to HER variation. The paper reports no significant robot-type differences in Study 2 at HER 0.5.

quotes.text: CommU, as a stylized robot with large, exag- gerated eyes and strong black white contrast, may create a persistent impression of being looked at across a broad range of eye directions.
In contrast, Nikola, being a highly human-like android with smaller, more realistic eyes, is likely to produce more perceptually salient gaze shifts, making variations in HER more impactful.
Regarding the robot types, no significant differences were found in both thinking and extroversion impressions.

fields.value: The paper analyzed human triadic conversation data and tested gaze-control videos for two robots, varying head-to-eye ratio and whether gaze aversions were timed to thinking. More head movement and thinking-aware gaze aversion increased perceived extroversion, while thinking-aware gaze also made the robots seem more as if they were thinking; effects of low head-to-eye ratios differed by robot appearance.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper frames gaze as a way to express internal state and personality, and describes role-based gaze allocation in triadic dialogue. It measures effects on perceived thinking and extroversion, details a layered gaze-control model, and compares a stylized robot with a humanlike android, including appearance-related differences in gaze impressions.
